column1: Every sensor wires to the left header (J1). Board TX goes to sensor RX, board RX to sensor TX. All grounds are common.

column9: Reasoning
The current TF03-series datasheet allows 5–24V. Taking power before the buck keeps the LiDAR's 480 mA peak off the board's regulator.
Serial signals only make sense if both ends share a ground.
GPIO17 is UART1's dedicated TX pin, which gives the cleanest timing. Board TX goes to sensor RX.
UART1's dedicated RX pin, the partner of GPIO17. The manual says not to leave TX or RX floating.

White/green are the CAN pair, not needed for UART. UART was chosen over CAN because CAN needs an extra transceiver chip. Colours follow the 5–24V version's six-wire cable (2024 TF03 UART/CAN manual); the old 5V version used brown RxD / yellow TxD.
The module has no overvoltage protection, so it must never see 5V.
Shared reference for the serial lines.
UART0 belongs to USB and UART1 to the LiDAR, so the GPS gets UART2. GPIO15 sits right before GPIO17 on J1.
Partner of GPIO15. UART is the GPS's factory default, needs two wires, and keeps it off any bus the IMU uses.
Once-per-second pulse aligned to GPS time, for timestamping readings precisely.
Lets the firmware hard-reset the GPS if it locks up. It has an internal pull-up, so leaving it unconnected is also safe.
The datasheet says to leave both open. Open D_SEL selects UART; SAFEBOOT_N is only for firmware recovery.
Rated 2.4–3.6V.
Shared reference for SPI.
GPIO10–13 are SPI2's dedicated pins, giving the fastest, most reliable SPI timing, and they sit in a row on J1.
Data from the board to the IMU.
SPI clock. Start at 1 MHz.
Data from the IMU to the board.
Goes low when the IMU has data waiting, so the board reads only when there's something to read. Required in SPI mode.
Lets the board restart the IMU cleanly.
Held high through reset to select SPI mode, then pulsed low to wake the IMU.
PS0 and PS1 both high selects SPI. SPI avoids I2C clock stretching, which the ESP32 handles poorly.
First free pin on J1 and not a strapping pin, so a press during power-up can't change how the board boots.
The internal pull-up holds GPIO4 high; a press pulls it low. No external resistor needed.
Runs at 3.3V, so its pull-ups sit at 3.3V and the I2C lines connect straight to the board. Confirm the module is rated for 3.3V; a 5V backpack would pull the lines to 5V.
Shared reference for I2C.
GPIO1 and GPIO2 sit side by side on J3 with no other job. The LCD gets its own I2C bus, separate from the IMU's SPI lines.
100 kHz is the PCF8574's maximum I2C speed. Default address 0x27 (0x3F on PCF8574A backpacks).
Feeds the board, whose own regulator makes 3.3V for the GPS, IMU and LCD. 5.1V leaves headroom for drop in the wires.
